steps: Declare a dtype with two named fields.
Build a one-row array from a tuple.
Select the score field and print it.
Structured arrays.realWorld: A row of mixed types — id, name, price — stays one record instead of three parallel arrays that can drift out of step.
mistakes: Passing a dict where a list of tuples is required.
Assuming field order can change after creation.
revision: A structured dtype names and types each field.
Field access returns a normal array, ready for reductions.

steps: Create a datetime64 array with a day unit.
Add an integer and print the result.
Note the unit decided what the integer means.
datetime64 arithmetic.realWorld: Due dates and retention windows are whole-day arithmetic, and integer addition is exact where float dates are not.
mistakes: Adding 1 to a [D] array expecting one second.
Mixing units in one array and getting a coarser resolution.
revision: The unit fixes what an integer step means.
Dates are stored as integers underneath, so addition is exact.

steps: Build an array of short strings.
Apply a char function to it.
Print the transformed array.
Vectorised string operations.realWorld: Normalising codes and stripping whitespace across a column is a char call, though real text work belongs in a proper text tool.
mistakes: Reaching for np.char for parsing or regex work.
Assuming the fixed width grows to fit the result.
revision: np.char applies string methods elementwise.
It suits tidy codes, not general text processing.

steps: Create a string array with a 2-character dtype.
Print the value.
Confirm the text was cut, not padded.
Fixed-width strings truncate.realWorld: A too-small string dtype silently loses characters, which is why a code column should be sized from the data, not guessed.
mistakes: Truncating identifiers or names during conversion.
Assuming the dtype will widen on assignment.
revision: A U<n> dtype stores at most n characters.
Overflow is cut at creation time.

steps: Build an array with a number, a string and None.
Print its dtype and one element.
Compare the dtype with a normal numeric array.
object dtype keeps Python objects.realWorld: Mixed or ragged data forces object dtype, and with it every fast numeric path is lost — a signal the data should be split.
mistakes: Using object dtype for numeric work and losing all speed.
Assuming comparisons and reductions behave normally.
revision: object dtype stores pointers to Python values.
Arithmetic falls back to Python and is far slower.

steps: Subtract two dates.
Print the difference and its unit.
Note it reports an interval, not a number.
timedelta64 tells the gap.realWorld: Dwell time and age calculations are differences, and the timedelta keeps the unit attached until you decide what to report.
mistakes: Adding a timedelta to a date of a different unit and losing precision.
Treating the printed value as a plain integer.
revision: Date minus date gives a timedelta64.
The unit comes from the operands.

steps: Compute a two-day difference.
Divide by a one-day timedelta.
Print the plain float 2.0.
Divide a timedelta to get a count.realWorld: Feeding a duration into a model needs a plain number, and dividing by the unit is the conversion that keeps the meaning clear.
mistakes: Casting the timedelta with astype and losing control of the unit.
Dividing by a plain 1 and leaving the result as a timedelta.
revision: Dividing by a unit timedelta yields a number.
Choose the unit to match what the report needs.

steps: Build a structured array with an id and a price.
Select the price field.
Sum it to show the field is a normal array.
Fields are read by name.realWorld: Revenue totals from a record table are a field selection plus a reduction, with no unpacking loop.
mistakes: Indexing by field number instead of name.
Expecting a field selection to copy the data.
revision: A field is read by name and comes back as an array.
All standard reductions then apply.

steps: Pass a short string array to a char function.
Print the result as a list.
Confirm every element was transformed.
char functions work elementwise on text.realWorld: Making category codes consistent before a group-by is one char call on the column.
mistakes: Writing a Python loop over the elements.
Expecting char functions to handle missing values gracefully.
revision: np.char methods apply to every element.
The result keeps the array's shape.

steps: Measure two strings of different lengths.
Print the integer array.
Note the fixed-width padding does not inflate the count.
str_len counts characters.realWorld: Validating that codes, postcodes or tickers are the right length is a str_len mask, not a per-row len call.
mistakes: Confusing the dtype width with the string length.
Assuming the result is a boolean mask.
revision: str_len returns the actual character count.
Padding is not counted.

steps: Create a start and an end date.
Subtract them to get a timedelta.
Convert to days and print the number.
Datetime differences are timedeltas.realWorld: Subscription length, SLA windows and cohort age are all day counts derived from two dates.
mistakes: Leaving the result as a timedelta and trying to average it.
Assuming the division changes the stored unit.
revision: Subtraction gives timedelta64.
Division by a unit timedelta gives a plain number.

steps: Declare a dtype with a text and an integer field.
Build one row from a tuple.
Print the score field.
A structured array reads fields by name.realWorld: Keeping a label beside its measurement in one row avoids a join later when the data is saved and reloaded.
mistakes: Exceeding the declared U4 width and losing characters.
Forgetting the dtype when constructing and getting a plain array.
revision: Each field has its own type and width.
Field access returns a normal array.

steps: Build a two-date array with a day unit.
Subtract the dates to get a timedelta.
Add a ten-day timedelta to the array.
Dates as datetime64.realWorld: Time series indexes and date filters work on datetime64 because comparison is just integer comparison.
mistakes: Expecting timezone handling; datetime64 carries no timezone.
Mixing [D] and [s] values and losing the finer unit.
revision: datetime64 is an integer on a chosen unit.
No timezone information is stored.

steps: Build two records with an id and a score.
List the field names.
Average the score field.
Structured arrays hold named fields.realWorld: A record table read from a CSV maps naturally onto named fields, and each field is immediately analysable.
mistakes: Treating the records as a 2-D numeric array.
Assuming names are mutable after the dtype is built.
revision: dtype.names lists the fields in order.
Each field reduces like any other array.

steps: Build an array with one NaN.
Locate it with isnan.
Average with nanmean and compare with plain mean.
NaN is not equal to anything.realWorld: One missing sensor reading can turn a whole dashboard average into NaN, which is why the nan-aware reductions exist.
mistakes: Using a == np.nan to find missing values.
Reporting the plain mean of a column with gaps.
revision: NaN never equals anything, including itself.
isnan locates it and nan- reductions skip it.

steps: Build an array with inf.
Test it with isinf.
Compare with isnan, which returns False for inf.
Infinity is a value, not a missing one.realWorld: Overflow and division by zero produce infinity, and treating it as missing hides the real bug that generated it.
mistakes: Assuming nan-aware functions also handle inf.
Clipping inf without asking why it appeared.
revision: inf is a valid float, not a missing marker.
isinf finds it; nan tests do not.

steps: Build a masked array with the middle element masked.
Average it and print the value.
Note the masked element was skipped.
Masked arrays carry their own mask.realWorld: Invalid readings stay visible in the data while reductions ignore them, which beats overwriting them with NaN.
mistakes: Expecting the mask to drop the element from the array.
Mixing masked and plain arrays and losing the mask.
revision: The mask travels with the data.
Reductions skip masked positions.

steps: Build an array with a NaN.
Apply isnan and print the boolean array.
Use it to count or filter the missing values.
isnan builds the mask.realWorld: Every cleaning step starts by counting the gaps, and isnan is the only reliable locator.
mistakes: Testing equality with nan.
Forgetting the mask's shape matches the source.
revision: isnan returns a boolean mask of the missing positions.
That mask composes with sum, ~ and indexing.

steps: Compute the plain mean of data with one NaN.
Compute nanmean of the same array.
Compare nan against 2.0.
nanmean ignores missing values.realWorld: Reporting an average from real data with gaps is a decision, and the two functions make the choice explicit.
mistakes: Using nanmean silently and hiding that data was missing.
Assuming nanmean handles inf as well.
revision: mean propagates NaN; nanmean skips it.
Always report how many values were skipped.

steps: Build an array with NaN and both infinities.
Apply nan_to_num and print the result.
Note each class of value has its own replacement.
nan_to_num replaces NaN and infinity.realWorld: A model that receives NaN produces NaN predictions, so the boundary is where non-finite values get replaced.
mistakes: Using the huge default for inf when a domain cap is needed.
Replacing values before diagnosing why they appeared.
revision: nan, posinf and neginf take separate replacements.
Defaults are 0 and the float maximum.

steps: Compare two arrays containing NaN with the default.
Repeat with equal_nan=True.
Print both answers.
allclose can treat NaN as equal.realWorld: Test assertions on data with gaps fail on NaN unless the comparison opts in, which is a common false alarm.
mistakes: Assuming allclose treats NaN as equal by default.
Leaving equal_nan off in a validation check.
revision: allclose compares with == underneath, so NaN fails.
equal_nan=True makes matching NaNs count as equal.

steps: Build an array with a NaN next to real values.
Print the position nanargmax returns.
Compare with argmax on the same data.
nanargmax skips NaN.realWorld: Picking the best non-missing record needs the nan-aware position, or the answer points at a gap.
mistakes: Using argmax and getting the NaN's position.
Calling nanargmax on an all-NaN slice, which raises.
revision: nanarg* ignores missing values when searching.
An all-missing input is an error, not a silent answer.

steps: Compare NaN with itself.
Print the result.
Explain the IEEE rule in one line.
NaN never equals itself.realWorld: Equality-based deduplication silently keeps every missing row, which is a bug that surfaces only in the row counts.
mistakes: Filtering missing values with != comparisons.
Using `in` or set membership to detect NaN.
revision: IEEE 754 defines NaN as unequal to everything.
Use isnan for detection.

steps: Build an array with one NaN.
Print the isnan mask as a list.
Sum it to count the missing values.
isnan finds missing values.realWorld: A data-quality report starts with one count per column, and a summed isnan mask supplies it.
mistakes: Forgetting the mask is invertible with ~.
Assuming isnan works on integer arrays — it needs a float dtype.
revision: isnan returns a boolean mask.
It composes with ~, sum and indexing.

steps: Compute std on data with a NaN.
Compute nanstd on the same data.
Print the rounded values and compare.
nanstd ignores the gaps.realWorld: Volatility and error bars computed from incomplete data need the nan-aware spread, or the whole metric collapses to NaN.
mistakes: Reporting nan as the spread rather than as a missing result.
Mixing nanmean with plain std on the same column.
revision: nan-prefixed reductions skip missing values.
Pair nanmean with nanstd so both describe the same rows.

steps: Build a mask of the missing values.
Invert it and index the array.
Average the filtered result.
Mask NaN, then reduce.realWorld: Filtering first gives the raw surviving values, which is what you need when the count of kept rows also matters.
mistakes: Forgetting the tilde and keeping only the NaNs.
Filtering a matrix elementwise and flattening the rows.
revision: ~np.isnan(a) keeps the valid values.
The filtered array works with any reduction, not just the nan ones.

steps: Mask the middle value of a three-element array.
Print the mean and the filled version.
Note filled replaced only the masked cell.
Masked arrays ignore invalid cells.realWorld: Keeping a sentinel visible in the data while excluding it from statistics is what a mask is for.
mistakes: Expecting masked values to be removed from indexing.
Forgetting filled() before writing the array out.
revision: Masked arrays carry a mask beside the values.
filled() substitutes the masked positions for output.

steps: Build an array with NaN and both infinities.
Replace them with domain-appropriate finite values.
Print the array and confirm no non-finite value remains.
nan_to_num replaces non-finite values.realWorld: Sorting and arithmetic behave unpredictably with non-finite values, so cleaning them at the boundary keeps every later step simple.
mistakes: Using the default inf replacement where the domain has a real cap.
Cleaning values that should have been rejected instead.
revision: nan, posinf and neginf are replaced independently.
The output contains only finite values.
